reading.rtitle: A Morning on the Credit Floor
paras: Camila Prado runs the credit desk of a digital bank in Belo Horizonte. Her bank has no branches, and every customer opens the account on a phone. She does not meet a single customer, and she says that is the whole point of the job. What she meets is data.

Her morning never changes. She opens the dashboard at seven, before the team arrives, and she reads three numbers first: how many requests arrived overnight, how many the model approved, and how many it declined. Rafael, the youngest analyst on the desk, reviews every case above ten thousand reais on his own. He sends her only the ones the model cannot explain, and she reads every one of them.

The model approves about eight requests out of ten, and it does that in less than a second. Camila prefers to talk about what it does not do. It does not write the rule, it does not choose the target, and it does not answer for a default. A person does all three, and in her bank that person is her.

On Friday morning she stops looking at the daily numbers. Nobody on her team changes a limit on a Friday, and that rule is hers. She says the mistakes she has seen in twelve years almost all happened on a Friday afternoon, in a hurry, on a case that somebody read once.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Brazilian digital-bank credit desk, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a person becomes a credit analyst in Brazil.
To show what one credit manager actually does in a normal morning, and what she leaves to the model.
To argue that digital banks should open branches again.

items.situation: Ask a question about Rafael, using the third person.

Not: Does he reviews. The -s goes to does, never to both.

items.situation: The text says her morning never changes. Where does never go in the sentence?
tips: Before the verb: she never changes her morning.
With to be it goes after: she is never late.

listenings.text: Let me tell you who does what on this team, because people always ask. Bruno opens the dashboard at seven, before anybody else arrives, and he reads the overnight numbers first. He does not decide anything on his own. He tells the rest of us what moved, and that is his job. Everything above ten thousand goes to a human, and the model handles the rest by itself. Paula reviews those cases, one by one, and she writes a line about each of them. And there is one thing I do not allow on this team. Nobody changes a limit without a written reason. Nobody. Three months later nobody remembers why the limit moved, and then we cannot explain the number to anybody who asks.

People ask me if a model is smart. That is the wrong question. A model is very good at one thing only: it repeats the same decision a million times without getting tired and without changing its mind. That is worth a lot of money, and it is also the danger. The model never asks whether the rule behind it is still the right rule. It cannot ask that. It only knows the world it learned from, and the world moves. So when the rule goes wrong, and one day it does, the model does not answer for it. The engineer who built it does not answer for it either. The person who wrote the policy answers for it, and that person has to read the numbers every week to know when the rule stopped working.
